enhanced_information: In gluconeogenesis, the reaction converting Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate to Fructose-6-phosphate requires a different enzyme than glycolysis. This is because gluconeogenesis uses the enzyme fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, whereas glycolysis uses phosphofructokinase-1 for the reverse reaction. The other reactions listed (2-phosphoglycerate to 3-phosphoglycerate, phosphoenolpyruvate to 2-phosphoglycerate, dihydroxyacetone phosphate to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, and 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate) use the same enzymes in both glycolysis and gluconeogenesis. analysis: In gluconeogenesis, certain steps require different enzymes than those used in glycolysis due to the need to bypass irreversible reactions. One such step is the conversion of Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate to Fructose-6-phosphate. In glycolysis, the reverse reaction (Fructose-6-phosphate to Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate) is catalyzed by phosphofructokinase-1, an irreversible step. In gluconeogenesis, this step is bypassed using the enzyme fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase. The other reactions listed either use the same enzymes in both pathways or are reversible reactions that do not require different enzymes. Therefore, the reaction that requires a different enzyme in gluconeogenesis compared to glycolysis is the conversion of Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate to Fructose-6-phosphate.
